narrative:
The model estimates a 42% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three factors stood out most in the decision. First, your overall career experience of more than 11 years across all jobs pushed the prediction strongly toward leaving. While only 15% of employees predicted to stay have this much total experience, the model sees long overall tenure as a sign that people are more likely to move on. Second, the number of training programs you attended in the last three years worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward staying. Attending seven or more programs is less common among those expected to remain, yet the model views this level of development activity as a positive signal of commitment. Third, your relatively short time in your current role—one to five years—again nudged the prediction toward leaving. This length of service in the present organization is actually the most typical range among people the model expects to stay, but in your specific combination of factors it still contributed to the higher risk score.

Taken together, your broad experience and shorter current tenure outweighed the positive effect of recent training. The organization should discuss retention plans with you, while you may want to reflect on whether your long-term career goals still align with this role.
